title: Part 1, Chapter 1
paragraphs: On an unbearably hot evening in early July, a young man stepped out of the tiny room he rented on S. Place and walked slowly, almost hesitantly, toward K. Bridge.

He had managed to avoid his landlady on the staircase. His room was tucked under the roof of a tall five-story building and was more like a closet than a proper room. The landlady, who provided him with the room, meals, and basic service, lived on the floor below. Every time he went out, he had to pass her kitchen, and the door was always open. Each time he walked by, the young man felt a wave of sickness and dread that made him grimace with shame. He was hopelessly in debt to her and terrified of running into her.

This was not because he was a coward -- far from it. But for some time now he had been in an agitated, irritable state bordering on nervous collapse. He had become so completely wrapped up in himself, so cut off from everyone, that he dreaded encountering not just his landlady but anyone at all. He was crushed by poverty, but lately even that had stopped weighing on him. He had given up dealing with practical matters entirely and had lost all desire to try. Nothing his landlady could actually do truly frightened him. But to be stopped on the stairs, forced to listen to her pointless gossip, her nagging demands for payment, her threats and complaints, to have to scramble for excuses, to dodge and lie -- no, he would rather creep down the stairs like a cat and slip out unseen.
This evening, however, stepping out into the street, he became sharply aware of his fear.

"I want to attempt a thing _like that_ and I'm scared of these little things," he thought with a strange smile. "Hm... yes, everything is in a man's hands, and he lets it all slip away out of cowardice -- that's a given. It would be interesting to know what people are most afraid of. Taking a new step, saying a new word -- that's what terrifies them most.... But I talk too much. I talk because I do nothing. Or maybe I do nothing because I talk. I've learned to talk this past month, lying around for days in my hole thinking... about fairy tales. Why am I going there now? Am I capable of _that_? Is _that_ serious? No, it's not serious at all. It's just a fantasy to entertain myself -- a game! Yes, maybe it's just a game."

The heat on the street was brutal -- the stagnant air, the crowds, the plaster, scaffolding, bricks, and dust everywhere, and that distinctive Petersburg stench so familiar to anyone who can't get out of the city in summer -- it all scraped painfully against the young man's already frayed nerves. The unbearable reek from the bars, which were especially numerous in this part of town, and the drunks he kept running into despite it being a workday, completed the picture of misery. A look of profound disgust flickered across the young man's fine features. He was, as it happened, exceptionally handsome -- taller than average, slim, well-built, with striking dark eyes and dark brown hair. Soon he sank into deep thought, or more accurately into a kind of mental blankness. He walked along without noticing his surroundings and without caring to. From time to time he would mutter something under his breath -- a habit of talking to himself that he had just acknowledged. In these moments he would realize that his thoughts were tangled and that he was very weak. He had barely eaten in two days.

He was so badly dressed that even someone accustomed to looking shabby would have been embarrassed to appear on the street in such rags. In this part of town, though, almost nothing you wore would raise an eyebrow. The proximity of the Hay Market, the abundance of disreputable establishments, and the predominantly working-class population crowded into these streets and alleys in the heart of Petersburg meant that every type of person could be seen here, and no figure, however bizarre, would cause surprise. But so much bitterness and contempt had built up in the young man's heart that, despite all the self-consciousness of youth, his rags bothered him least of all on the street. Running into acquaintances or former classmates was another matter -- he hated that at any time. And yet when a drunk being hauled somewhere in a massive wagon pulled by a heavy draft horse suddenly yelled at him from the road -- "Hey, you! German hat man!" -- bellowing and pointing at him, the young man froze and clutched his hat in a panic. It was a tall round hat from Zimmerman's, but completely worn out, faded with age, full of holes and stains, brimless and bent to one side in the most ridiculous way. It was not shame, however, but something closer to terror that seized him.

"I knew it," he muttered in confusion. "I knew it! That's the worst of all! Some stupid thing like this, the most trivial detail, could ruin the whole plan. Yes, my hat is too noticeable.... It looks ridiculous, and that makes it noticeable.... With these rags I should be wearing a cap, any kind of old flat thing, not this grotesque hat. Nobody wears a hat like this -- you'd spot it a mile away, you'd remember it.... The point is that people would remember it, and that would give them a lead. For this kind of thing you need to be as invisible as possible.... Details, details are what matter! It's always the little things that ruin everything...."

He did not have far to go. He knew exactly how many steps it was from his front gate: seven hundred and thirty. He had counted them once, lost in daydreams. At the time he had not believed in those dreams and was only tormenting himself with their horrifying audacity. Now, a month later, he had begun to see them differently. Despite all his internal monologues mocking his own weakness and indecision, he had unconsciously come to see this "horrifying" dream as something to be attempted -- though he still did not fully admit this to himself. He was going now for a "rehearsal" of his plan, and with every step his agitation grew more intense.

With his heart pounding and his hands trembling, he approached a large building that faced the canal on one side and the street on the other. The building was divided into small apartments and housed all kinds of working people -- tailors, locksmiths, cooks, various Germans, girls scraping together a living however they could, petty clerks, and so on. People were constantly coming and going through the two gates and across the two courtyards. Three or four doormen worked in the building. The young man was relieved not to run into any of them, and immediately slipped unnoticed through the right-hand door and up the staircase. It was a back staircase, dark and narrow, but he already knew it well and liked these surroundings -- in this kind of darkness, even the nosiest eyes were nothing to worry about.

"If I'm this scared now, what would it be like if I were actually going to do it?" he couldn't help thinking as he reached the fourth floor. Some movers blocked his way, carrying furniture out of an apartment. He knew a German civil servant and his family had lived there. So this German was moving out, which meant the fourth floor on this staircase would be empty except for the old woman. "That's a good thing, at least," he thought as he rang the bell of the old woman's apartment. The bell made a faint tinkling sound, as if it were tin rather than copper. The small apartments in buildings like these always have bells that sound like that. He had forgotten the sound of this bell, and now its peculiar tinkling seemed to remind him of something, bringing it sharply into focus.... He flinched -- his nerves were completely shot by now. After a moment, the door opened a crack. The old woman peered at her visitor through the gap with obvious suspicion, and nothing was visible but her small eyes, glinting in the darkness. But when she saw other people on the landing, she grew bolder and opened the door wide. The young man stepped into the dark entryway, which was separated from the tiny kitchen by a partition. The old woman stood before him in silence, studying him with a questioning look. She was a tiny, shriveled woman of about sixty, with sharp, hostile eyes and a sharp little nose. Her colorless, somewhat graying hair was heavily greased with oil, and she wore nothing on her head. Around her thin, long neck -- which looked like a chicken's leg -- she had a flannel rag knotted, and despite the heat, a moth-eaten fur cape, yellowed with age, hung loosely from her shoulders. The old woman coughed and groaned constantly. The young man must have looked at her with an unusual expression, because a flash of suspicion returned to her eyes.
"Raskolnikov, a student. I was here a month ago," the young man said quickly, with a slight bow, remembering he needed to be more polite.
"I remember, sir. I remember your visit perfectly well," the old woman said clearly, keeping her searching eyes fixed on his face.

"And here... I am again, on the same business," Raskolnikov continued, slightly thrown and surprised by the old woman's suspicion. "Maybe she's always like this and I just didn't notice it last time," he thought uneasily.
The old woman paused as if considering, then stepped aside and pointed toward the door of the room, letting her visitor go ahead of her.
"Come in, sir."
The small room the young man entered had yellow wallpaper, geraniums and muslin curtains in the windows, and at that moment was brightly lit by the setting sun.

"So the sun will be shining like this _then_ too!" flashed through Raskolnikov's mind almost involuntarily, and he quickly scanned the room, trying to memorize the layout as thoroughly as possible. But there was nothing remarkable about it. The furniture, all very old and made of yellow wood, consisted of a sofa with a large arched back, an oval table in front of it, a vanity table with a mirror between the windows, chairs along the walls, and two or three cheap prints in yellow frames showing German girls holding birds -- that was all. In the corner, a small lamp burned in front of an icon. Everything was spotlessly clean; the floor and furniture were polished to a shine.
"Lizaveta's doing," the young man thought. There wasn't a speck of dust anywhere in the apartment.

"You find this kind of cleanliness in the homes of bitter old widows," Raskolnikov thought, and he glanced curiously at the cotton curtain over the doorway to the other tiny room, where the old woman's bed and dresser were -- a room he had never looked into before. These two rooms were the entire apartment.
"What do you want?" the old woman said sharply, coming into the room and standing before him as before, so she could look him straight in the face.
"I've brought something to pawn," he said, and pulled from his pocket an old-fashioned flat silver watch with a globe engraved on the back and a steel chain.
"But the term on your last pledge has expired. It was due the day before yesterday."
"I'll bring you the interest for another month. Just wait a little."
"Whether I wait or sell your pledge right now -- that's for me to decide, sir."
"How much will you give me for the watch, Alyona Ivanovna?"
"You bring me such worthless things, sir -- it's barely worth anything. Last time I gave you two rubles for your ring, and you could buy one brand new at a jeweler's for a ruble and a half."
"Give me four rubles for it. I'll redeem it -- it was my father's. I'll have money soon."
"A ruble and a half, interest in advance, take it or leave it!"
"A ruble and a half!" the young man cried.

"Take it or leave it." The old woman held the watch back out to him. The young man took it and was so angry he almost walked out, but caught himself immediately, remembering there was nowhere else to go -- and that he had come here with another purpose as well.
"Hand it over," he said roughly.

The old woman fumbled in her pocket for her keys and disappeared behind the curtain into the other room. Left standing alone in the middle of the room, the young man listened intently, thinking. He could hear her unlocking the dresser.

"Must be the top drawer," he thought. "So she keeps the keys in a pocket on the right side. All on one bunch, on a steel ring.... And there's one key that's three times bigger than the others, with deep notches. That can't be for the dresser... so there must be some other chest or strongbox... That's worth knowing. Strongboxes always have keys like that... But how degrading all this is."
The old woman came back.

"Here you are, sir: at ten kopecks per ruble per month, that's fifteen kopecks from a ruble and a half for the month in advance. And for the two rubles I lent you before, you owe me twenty kopecks on the same terms, in advance. That comes to thirty-five kopecks total. So for the watch I give you one ruble and fifteen kopecks. Here."
"What! Only a ruble and fifteen kopecks now!"
"That's right."

The young man didn't argue and took the money. He looked at the old woman and was in no hurry to leave, as if there were still something he wanted to say or do, though he himself didn't quite know what.
"I might bring you something else in a day or two, Alyona Ivanovna -- something valuable -- silver -- a cigarette case, as soon as I get it back from a friend..." He trailed off awkwardly.
"Well, we'll talk about it then, sir."
"Goodbye -- are you always home alone? Your sister isn't here with you?" he asked as casually as he could, stepping into the hallway.
"What business is she of yours, sir?"
"Oh, nothing special, I was just asking. You jump to conclusions too quickly.... Good day, Alyona Ivanovna."

Raskolnikov left in a state of total confusion. The confusion only deepened as he went. He stopped short on the stairs two or three times, as if struck by a sudden thought. Out on the street he burst out: "Oh God, how disgusting this all is! And can I, can I really.... No, that's insane, that's ridiculous!" he said firmly. "How could such a monstrous idea enter my head? What filth my heart is capable of. Yes, filth above all -- vile, revolting, disgusting! -- and for a whole month I've been...." But no words or exclamations could express his turmoil. The wave of revulsion that had begun building in his chest on the way to the old woman's had now reached such intensity, taken such definite shape, that he didn't know what to do with himself to escape his misery. He stumbled along the sidewalk like a drunk, bumping into people, and only came to his senses on the next street. Looking around, he realized he was standing near a tavern that you entered by going down steps from the sidewalk to a basement. At that moment two drunks came out the door, cursing and propping each other up as they climbed the steps. Without a second thought, Raskolnikov went down the steps. He had never been in a tavern before, but now he felt dizzy and was burning with thirst. He wanted a cold beer and blamed his sudden weakness on not having eaten. He sat down at a sticky little table in a dark, dirty corner, ordered a beer, and gulped down the first glass. He felt better immediately, and his thoughts cleared.

"That's all nonsense," he said with a surge of hope, "there's nothing to worry about! It's just physical weakness. One glass of beer, a piece of dry bread -- and in a second the brain is sharper, the mind is clearer, the will is strong! God, how pathetic all this is!"

Despite this contemptuous dismissal, he was already looking cheerful, as if suddenly freed from a terrible weight, and he glanced around at the other people in the room with something like warmth. But even in that moment, he had a vague sense that this lighter mood was not normal either.

There were only a few people left in the tavern. Besides the two drunks he had passed on the steps, a group of about five men and a girl with an accordion had left at the same time. After they went, the room felt quiet and half-empty. The remaining customers were a man who looked like a tradesman, drunk but not falling down, sitting in front of a mug of beer, and his companion -- a huge, heavyset man with a gray beard wearing a short coat. This one was very drunk and had dozed off on the bench. Every so often, as if in his sleep, he would crack his fingers, arms spread wide, his torso bouncing on the bench, while he hummed some pointless tune, trying to recall words that went something like:
"His wife a year he fondly loved, His wife a -- a year he -- fondly loved."
Or suddenly waking up again:
"Walking along the crowded row, He met the one he used to know."

But nobody shared his amusement. His silent companion watched these outbursts with open hostility and suspicion. There was one other man in the room who looked like a retired government clerk. He sat by himself, taking an occasional sip from his mug and glancing around at the others. He, too, seemed agitated about something.
